51	The plan specifies *"when on, opening a look after 18:00 local logs it."* **Rejected — opening a look is
52	not wearing it.** `wear_logs` is the foundation of cost-per-wear, streaks, most-worn, gathering-dust and
53	gap analysis, i.e. of everything Pro sells. Logging views as wears inflates all of it permanently, with
54	no way afterwards to tell a fabricated wear from a real one — poisoning the paid feature to save one tap.
55	`MONETISATION.md` §1: *"they pay for it in month three, once the data is theirs."*
56	
57	**Build an evening confirmation instead** (agreed with the user 2026-08-05): if you opened a look today
58	and logged nothing, ask once — *"Did you wear <look> today?"* — **Yes / No**. Yes writes the same row the
59	button writes; No writes nothing and it does not ask again that day. Triggers when the app is next opened
60	after ~18:00 local, so it needs no web-push and is buildable now.

62	Two details that decide whether it helps or hurts: **Yes and No must be equally easy** (a lone "Yes" with
63	a dismiss ✕ gets tapped to clear it, and the data inflates anyway), and it asks only about looks actually
64	opened, most recent first — dwell time is not tracked, so "most recent" is the honest simple choice.

23	## 1. The principle: meter what costs us money, sell what compounds
24	
25	Two different things can justify a price, and confusing them is how apps end up gating their own growth.
26	
27	- **Cost-to-serve.** Every AI generation costs real money. That is a *meter*, and metering it is honest.
28	- **Compounding value.** Analytics, planning, advice. Zero marginal cost, high willingness to pay,
29	  and — importantly — *worthless to a new user*. Nobody pays for cost-per-wear on day one; they pay for
30	  it in month three, once the data is theirs.
31	
32	Everything else stays free. In particular, three things must **never** be gated:
33	
34	| Never gate | Why |
35	|---|---|
36	| **The daily drop + the "why"** | It is the product. Gating it means nobody discovers the magic. |
37	| **The Style DNA share card** | It is a growth channel, not a feature. Charging for your own marketing is self-harm. |
38	| **Tagging, item editing, and the closet's *quality*** | The closet is the moat and the switching cost. Every item added makes the product better *and* makes leaving harder. **Amended 2026-08-05:** a generous SIZE cap (50, see §2) is now in place, but nothing about how a closet works is gated — no reduced tagging, no locked fields, no degraded stylist. The cap is a ceiling on quantity, never on capability. |
39	
40	---
41	
42	## 2. The meter: three rerolls a day
43	
44	> **AMENDED 2026-08-04.** This section previously read *"Free gets 3 AI generations per day"*, counting
45	> the daily drop toward that three. **It contradicted §1 of this same document**, which says the daily
46	> drop must never be gated — with drops counted, a free user who has viewed three occasions is refused
47	> the fourth, which is precisely gating the drop. §1 is what matches Decision 4 in `CLAUDE.md`, so §2 is
48	> the part that gave. The old wording is also what `2026-07-22-regenerate-quota.md` disagreed with; all
49	> three documents now say the same thing.
50	
51	**Every occasion's first look of the day is free, on every tier. Free gets three rerolls a day, pooled
52	across all occasions. Pro rerolls without limit.**
53	
54	> **Pooled, not per-occasion** (decided 2026-08-05). A per-occasion allowance was built first and
55	> reverted: most people care about ONE occasion on a given day, so rationing per occasion is strictest
56	> exactly where attention goes and generous where nobody is looking — you could be refused a second Work
57	> reroll while holding an unused Evening one you never wanted. The usual objection to a shared pool, that
58	> it can block an occasion you have not opened, **does not apply once drops are free**: tapping a new
59	> occasion is always a drop, so the pool only ever meters rerolls.
60	
61	A "generation" is any call that spends a model request. There are three kinds, and they are metered
62	differently:
63	
64	| Kind | Free | Pro |
65	|---|---|---|
66	| **`drop`** — an occasion's first look of the day | Always free | Always free |
67	| **`regenerate`** — asking an occasion again | 3 per day, all occasions | Unlimited |
68	| **`styled`** — building a look around a chosen piece | Gated (Pro #2) | Unlimited |
69	
70	Reading a look that already exists is always free and always unlimited, per Decision 5 — including
71	re-opening a styled look, which is cached per (user, item, local day).
72	
73	The limit bites at the honest moment: someone rerolling a third time is genuinely dissatisfied, which is
74	when "Pro rerolls without limit" is a fair offer rather than a toll.
75	
76	**No counter is displayed** (decided 2026-08-05). The user is not told how many rerolls remain before
77	they run out. A visible "1 left" badge makes every free user think about the limit constantly, which is
78	the opposite of this section's design — *a user who never thinks about the limit never hits it*.
79	
80	### The ceiling, which is the number that matters
81	
82	Four occasion drops plus three rerolls:
83	
84	```
85	7 × $0.003 = $0.021/day  →  $0.63/user/month absolute worst case
86	```
87	
88	Realistic use is 2–3 generations a day, so ≈ $0.20/month. **The ceiling is the point:** a free tier needs
89	a worst case you can survive, and it must not scale with closet size. This is why `styled` is Pro rather
90	than "first time per item free" — the latter has no ceiling at all, since a 150-item closet would permit
91	150 free generations a day, and it would leave nothing in Pro #2 to sell.
92	
93	### The arithmetic, so the number is not a vibe
94	
95	Haiku 4.5 at $1/1M in, $5/1M out. One text-only re-rank ≈ 1,500 in + 300 out:
96	
97	```
98	(1500 / 1M × $1) + (300 / 1M × $5) = $0.0015 + $0.0015 ≈ $0.003 per generation
99	```
100	
101	| Scenario | Cost/user/month |
102	|---|---|
103	| Free user, realistic ~1.5 generations/day | **≈ $0.14** |
104	| Free user maxing the ceiling — 7/day | **≈ $0.63** |
105	| Pro user, heavy — 10/day | **≈ $0.90** (vs €5 revenue) |
106	
107	Item tagging is one-time and negligible: a 100-item closet is ~$0.20, ever.
108	
109	### Closet size: 50 pieces free (decided 2026-08-05)
110	
111	**A free closet holds 50 pieces. Pro is unlimited.**
112	
113	A 10-per-day rate limit was built first and removed in favour of this: with a ceiling in place the rate
114	was redundant, and two overlapping rules made the free tier feel meaner than it is — a new user would
115	have needed five days to reach 50, throttled during exactly the days you want them filling their closet.
116	One rule is easier to explain and easier to sell against.
117	
118	**The cap counts UNARCHIVED pieces.** Nothing in the product deletes an item, so counting archived ones
119	would strand a user at the cap with no way back under it. Archiving is the intended way to make room,
120	and an archived piece is not in your closet by any reading of the word.
121	
122	This section previously read *"Do not cap closet size"* full stop. What survives of that reasoning, and
123	why **50** rather than a tighter number:
124	
125	- **Storage does not justify a total cap.** Measured on the real local closet: `original.jpg` averages
126	  233 kB and `cutout.webp` 97 kB, so **330 kB per item**. A 100-item closet is 33 MB; 10,000 free users
127	  with full closets is ~330 GB, about **$4.83/month**. The far bigger lever is queue #13
128	  `cutout-backfill` — 10 legacy `cutout.png` files still average ~700 kB, 7× their WebP equivalent.
129	- **A LOW cap would degrade the product rather than gate it.** PR #15 measured a 21-item closet at **21
130	  combos in winter against 48 in summer**; PR #14 exists because small closets starve the candidate
131	  pool. Cap items at 20–30 and free users judge the stylist on a wardrobe too thin for it to work —
132	  selling a worse magic moment rather than fewer features. **50 sits clear of that range**, so a free
133	  closet is a full one with a ceiling, not a starved one.
134	- §1's reasoning still holds directionally: the closet is the moat and the switching cost, which is why
135	  the cap is generous rather than the 20-ish figure common in this category.
136	
137	The limit is enforced in `uploadAndTag`, not `confirmItem`: the two storage writes and the tagging call
138	all happen before the confirm screen, so a check at confirm would already have paid for the item it
139	refuses.
140	
141	At 5% conversion, 100 users cost roughly $14–27/month to serve and return ~€25. Thin but positive — and
142	Pro users are cheap to serve relative to what they pay, which is the right shape. **If real usage runs
143	above ~2 generations/day for free users, lower the free allowance to 2 before raising the price.**
144	
145	---
146	
147	## 3. The tiers
148	
149	### Free — the whole loop, forever
150	
151	- **Up to 50 closet pieces** (unarchived), with full AI tagging, background removal and item editing —
152	  the cap is on quantity, never on capability
153	- The daily drop: **every** occasion's looks with the one-sentence why, never rationed
154	- **3 rerolls per day**, pooled across all occasions
155	- Per-item wear facts on the item detail screen (times worn, cost-per-wear, last worn) — the *screen*
156	  that analyses the whole wardrobe is Pro #4; a fact about the piece you are looking at is not
157	- Wear logging, the Fit Diary, streaks — *the habit loop is what creates a payer*
158	- Style DNA card and sharing
159	- Up to **10 saved outfits**
160	- Weather, location, rain guard, all preferences
161	
162	### Pro — €5/mo
163	
164	| # | Feature | Type | Source |
165	|---|---|---|---|
166	| # | Feature | Type | Source |
167	|---|---|---|---|
168	| 1 | **Unlimited rerolls** — reroll freely, any occasion | Meter | Design (*"unlimited daily looks"*) |
169	| 2 | **Style an outfit with this** — build a look around any piece, unlimited | Meter | New |
170	| 3 | **Packing mode** — a trip in, a capsule and per-day looks out | Meter + planning | Design |
171	| 4 | **Cost-per-wear analytics** — the full Wear Stats screen | Compounding | Design |
172	| 5 | **Gap analysis** — *"a camel overcoat unlocks 14 new outfits"* | Compounding | New |
173	| 6 | **Unlimited saved outfits + favourites** | Compounding | New |
174	| 7 | **Unlimited closet size** — past the free 50 | Ceiling | New (2026-08-05) |
175	
176	Items 1, 3 and 4 are the design's own three. The rest are what turn them into a bundle worth a recurring
177	charge rather than a single metered button.
178	
179	> **Packing mode is advertised before it exists, deliberately** (user, 2026-08-05). The entitlement
180	> (`packingMode`) and the pitch copy both name it; the feature is scoping-only
181	> (`plans/scoping/2026-07-24-packing-mode-scoping.md`, seven open decisions). This is acceptable **while
182	> in development and while nobody can pay** — no checkout exists. ⚠️ **It must be built before Pro is
183	> actually sold**, or the copy has to drop it: charging for a named feature that does not exist is the
184	> one version of this that is not acceptable.
185	
186	### Why gap analysis is the sharpest one
187	
188	It is the only feature that answers *"what should I buy?"* — the highest-intent question a wardrobe app
189	can be asked. It is also the natural home for the design's **"See curated picks"** CTA (`:767`), which
190	makes it the bridge to a second revenue line. It is deliberately Pro from day one so that affiliate
191	revenue never becomes a reason to degrade the free experience.
192	
193	### Why packing mode earns its place
194	
195	It is the only Pro feature with a hard deadline attached — you need it *this week, before the flight* —
196	which converts far better than an open-ended benefit. It is episodic, so it does not inflate steady-state
197	cost, and it is the most screenshot-shareable output the product could produce.
198	
199	**Packing mode does not exist in any spec, design or plan.** It needs a brainstorm before a plan; see §5.
200	
201	---
202	
203	## 4. What this means for the code
204	
205	**Everything Pro must route through one seam.** Gating six screens by retrofitting `if (isPro)` into
206	each is how this becomes unmaintainable — and it is exactly the fork where this project's stated
207	preference is the extensible option, not the minimal diff.
208	
209	`lib/outfits/quota.ts` is already that seam for generations (`assertCanGenerate` currently returns
210	unconditionally). It needs to widen into `lib/billing/entitlements.ts` covering both meters and
211	capabilities:
212	
213	```ts
214	type Entitlements = {
215	  tier: Tier;
216	  /** Per occasion, per day. null = unlimited. Drops themselves are never metered. */
217	  regeneratesPerOccasion: number | null;
218	  /** "Style an outfit with this" — Pro #2. */
219	  styledLooks: boolean;
220	  savedOutfits: number | null;
221	  analytics: boolean;                 // the Wear Stats SCREEN, not the item tile
222	  gapAnalysis: boolean;
223	  packingMode: boolean;
224	};
225	```
226	
227	> **AMENDED 2026-08-04:** this was `generationsPerDay: number | null`, matching the superseded §2. A
228	> single daily number cannot express "drops are always free, regenerates are capped per occasion", and
229	> counting stored `outfits` rows cannot implement it either — a regenerate *replaces* the day's rows for
230	> an occasion, so afterwards a first drop and a fifth are indistinguishable. Hence the
231	> `generation_events` ledger, pulled forward from `2026-07-22-regenerate-quota.md`.
232	
233	Two hard rules:
234	
235	1. **"Limited" is a state, not an error.** A user at their daily limit sees an explanation and an
236	   upgrade path, never a thrown exception or a blank screen. This is already the stated design of the
237	   regenerate-quota plan; it now applies everywhere.
238	2. **Read entitlements server-side only.** A client-side check is a suggestion.
239	
240	Until billing exists, `entitlements()` returns the free tier for everyone, with a local override so Pro
241	surfaces can be built and tested. **No Stripe until the features are worth paying for.**
242	
243	---
244	
245	## 5. Plan order, revised for this
246	
247	Two new plans, and one insertion point that matters.
248	
249	**`entitlements` must land before any Pro-gated feature is built.** Wear stats, gap analysis, saved
250	outfits and packing mode are all gated; building them first means retrofitting the gate into four
251	screens afterwards.
252	
253	| # | Plan | Status | Tier impact |
254	|---|---|---|---|
255	| 1 | `seasons-soft-preference` | written | — |
256	| 2 | `design-tokens` | written | — |
257	| 3 | `item-data-completeness` | written | price → cost-per-wear |
258	| 4 | `outfit-detail-wear-logging` | written | wear data → all analytics |
259	| 5 | `item-detail-rebuild` | written | ships Pro feature #2 behind the seam |
260	| 6 | `fit-diary` | written | free (retention) |
261	| 7 | **`entitlements`** | **to write** | **the seam — blocks 8, 10, 11** |
262	| 8 | `regenerate-quota` | **rewrite** | becomes Pro #1; 3/day free |
263	| 9 | `profile-hub` → `settings` | written | Pro card gets a real state |
264	| 10 | `wear-stats` | written — **add the gate** | Pro #4 + #5 |
265	| — | ~~`packing-mode`~~ | **deferred — scoping only** | Pro #3 in the tier above, but out of the build queue until its open decisions are discussed. See `plans/scoping/2026-07-24-packing-mode-scoping.md`. **The tier's marketing copy names it, so it cannot ship as a Pro selling point until it exists** — either build it before charging, or sell Pro on the other five. |
266	| 12 | `item-signals-in-generator` | written | — |
267	| 13 | `cutout-backfill` | written | — |
268	| 14 | `route-url-audit` | written | runs last |
269	| 15 | `generator-audit` | written | last before billing |
270	| 16 | *billing / Stripe* | not scoped | after 1–15 |
271	
272	Note the ordering consequence: **`item-detail-rebuild` (5) ships a Pro feature before the seam exists
273	(7).** Either move the seam earlier, or have that plan call `assertCanGenerate` — which already exists —
274	and let the entitlements plan widen it underneath. **The second is cheaper and is the recommendation.**
275	
276	---
277	
278	## 6. Not yet tiered
279	
280	- **Talk to the stylist** (`plans/scoping/2026-07-24-stylist-chat-scoping.md`) — free-text intent
281	  ("outdoor wedding, 28°") or an actual chat. Which tier it lands in depends entirely on which of those
282	  two it is: one-shot intent extraction costs about **a third of a generation** and fits inside the free
283	  3/day meter; a multi-turn conversation resends its history every turn, so cost grows quadratically and
284	  it would have to be **Pro and turn-capped**. Decide the feature before deciding its tier.
285	
286	## 7. Open questions
287	
288	- **Annual pricing.** €5/mo implies roughly €48/yr at the usual discount. Not decided.
289	- **Trial.** A 14-day Pro trial after the fifth wear log would land when the analytics finally have data
290	  to show. Not decided.
291	- **Regional pricing.** Euro is the design's currency; the app targets the EU and Supabase is EU-region.
292	  Needs a decision alongside the currency setting in Settings.
293	- **"See curated picks."** Affiliate partner, disclosure requirements, and whether recommendations may
294	  ever influence what the stylist suggests. **They must not** — the moment purchase incentives touch
295	  outfit ranking, the one-sentence why stops being trustworthy, and that sentence is the product.

Read all four. Here's where things stand and what I'd want decided before writing any code.

## State (verified against git, not the docs)

`main` = `6de4730`, tree clean, no open PRs, nothing in flight. STATE.md's narrative matches git — it's current.

Queue #1–#9a are all merged (PRs #16, #18, #19, #20, #22, #23, #25, #27). **Next is #9b `settings`.**

`BUGS.md` is the 2026-07-04 review and is almost entirely historical — #1–#4 (tagging schema, body limit, lazy Anthropic client, swallowed upload errors), #5 (404 nav tabs), #9 (editable tags) and #14 (triplicated vocab) have all shipped since. I'd treat it as an archive, not a worklist.

## The settings plan is stale in five places

I read it against the code. It cannot be executed as written:

1. **Task 4 Step 4 — auto-log.** Already rejected (README, agreed with you 2026-08-05): opening a look isn't wearing it, and `wear_logs` is what all of Pro's analytics is built on. Must be cut, and `autoLogWorn` comes out of `PreferencesSchema` and its tests along with it.
2. **Task 5 Step 3 says "inert Pro banner (£5/mo)."** Price is €5, and PR #27 shipped `components/billing/pro-card.tsx` + the shared `UpgradeSheet`. Settings should reuse them or drop the banner — a second hand-rolled inert banner is exactly the divergence the shared sheet exists to prevent.
3. **Task 4's rain-guard signature.** `lib/generator/rules.ts:104` is still `weatherRules(w: Weather)` — one arg. The plan's three tests are correct as written, and the heat list is present, so its third test stays.
4. **Sign-out.** `app/profile/page.tsx:71` holds it with a comment saying the design moves it to Settings. That move is real work in this plan, not a note.
5. **Toggle count.** With auto-log gone, Settings ships **one** live toggle: rain guard.

## Two decisions I want from you before coding

**1. Is one live toggle enough to be a screen?** With auto-log removed, `/settings` is: account row, one working switch, a disabled DE control, a read-only location row, a read-only °C row, a Pro card, and sign-out. That's a real screen (sign-out has to live somewhere, and the `preferences` jsonb column is the seam every future toggle needs), but it's thinner than the plan assumed. The alternative is to skip ahead and take **#11 `styled-look-depth` Task 1** first — the README calls it independent and "a cheap real quality win": the styled shortlist skips `diversify`, so the model picks between 20 variations of one idea. That's a visible quality bug in a Pro feature. Settings is plumbing; #11 Task 1 makes the product better. I'd do #11 Task 1 first, then Settings.

**2. The evening wear-confirmation — its own plan now, or later?** You and I agreed it replaces auto-log: after ~18:00, if you opened a look and logged nothing, ask once, *Yes / No*, equally weighted. It's genuinely the better feature and it feeds the data Pro sells. But it's a new surface with real design questions (where does the prompt live — a sheet? the diary?), so it wants a brainstorm, not a task bolted onto Settings. My call: write it as a separate small plan, but not this session unless you want it.

content.text:
Confirmed 1, 2, 4. Point 3 explained, and one real problem with 5.

## Point 3, plainly

That one wasn't a staleness item — it was me checking the plan's starting assumption still holds. Task 4 says "give `weatherRules` a second argument so it can be told whether rain guard is on." I looked: `lib/generator/rules.ts:104` is still `weatherRules(w: Weather)`, one argument. So the plan's three tests are correct as written and nothing needs changing. Nothing for you to decide — I should have just said "checked, still fine."

## Point 5 — two of your three are cheap, one is not

**Rain guard** — settled, ships.

**Metric units °C/°F** — the plan said don't ship it. **The plan is wrong and I'll build it.** I traced every temperature in the codebase: the generator's thresholds are Celsius physics (`HOT_C = 25`, outerwear below 15°) and must stay Celsius, but the display sites are only five — `weather-strip.tsx` ×3, `advice.ts`, and `outfits/[id]/page.tsx`. So it's a `formatTemp(tempC, unit)` helper at the render boundary plus threading one preference. An hour of work, fully honest. The model prompt in `rerank.ts` stays °C deliberately — that's internal, not something you read.

**Daily fit reminder** — this one I can't build honestly right now, and here's the concrete reason rather than the plan's hand-wave. There is **no service worker in the project at all**: `public/` has none, the manifest has no push config, no VAPID keys, no subscription table, no scheduler. A daily reminder at 8am local needs all five of those plus a cron that knows each user's timezone. And a caveat specific to us: **iOS delivers web push only to PWAs actually installed to the home screen** — for anyone using Fitcheck in a Safari tab, the switch would be on and silently do nothing, which is the exact failure the plan's own rule is about.

**My recommendation: it goes in the wear-confirmation plan, not Settings.** You've already put that plan immediately after this one, and it's the same feature — the evening confirmation is "nudge the user at a time of day," the fit reminder is "nudge the user at a time of day." One notification mechanism, built once, serving both. Building push inside Settings means building it twice.

That gives Settings **two live toggles that both work** (rain guard, units), and the reminder ships a plan later with the machinery it actually needs.

If you'd rather I build web-push now and have Settings carry all three, say so and I'll do it — but it's a multi-day piece pulled out of Phase 2, and it makes Settings a notifications project.

## Ordering — does it matter?

You asked what the difference is. Technically: **almost none.** They share no files — Settings touches `profiles.preferences`, `app/settings/`, `lib/profile/`, and one signature in `rules.ts`; look-depth Task 1 touches only `style-actions.ts` to add the missing `diversify` call. No dependency in either direction.

But there's one asymmetry that decides it: **the wear-confirmation plan you want next needs `profiles.preferences` to exist** — at minimum for "don't ask again today," probably for an opt-out too. Settings creates that column. So Settings first puts the thing you asked for next directly behind its prerequisite, and look-depth Task 1 is small enough that waiting costs it nothing.

**Settings → look-depth → wear-confirmation**, unless you want the quick win merged first.

Give me the nod on the reminder and I'll branch `feat/settings` and start.
go, i like it, so we need to build whole notification system?

Quick correction on my own framing, because it changes what you're signing up for:

**The wear-confirmation feature needs no notification system at all.** It triggers when the app is next opened after ~18:00 local — it's an in-app prompt, zero push, buildable today. I lumped it together with the reminder last message; that was sloppy.

So it's only the **daily fit reminder** that needs the push stack, and it's the only thing in the product that does. That stack is: a service worker, VAPID keypair, a `push_subscriptions` table, a permission-request flow, and a scheduled sender that fires per-user at their local morning. Plus the iOS constraint — installed-PWA only. It's a genuine multi-day project for one switch, which is why it's worth its own plan and not a task inside this one.

79	 * Whether a wool garment suits 30°C is decided by its weight and weave, not its
80	 * fibre: tropical, fresco and high-twist wools are summer suiting, and merino is
81	 * used *for* heat because it wicks and breathes. `items.material` is a bare
82	 * fibre name today, so a "wool" rule cannot tell a summer-weight trouser from a
83	 * melton coat — it would exclude exactly the smart-casual work wear this app is

Confirmed **pre-existing on `main`** and unrelated to my change: with 1 top / 1 bottom / 2 shoes the walk emits the same combo twice and `s2` is unreachable.

Root cause is the shoe stride at `candidates.ts:176` — `shoes[(t + d * 2) % shoes.length]`. When there's one top, `t` is always 0, so the index is `2d % shoes.length`, which is permanently 0 whenever `shoes.length` is 2. PR #14 measured shoe coverage on a 20-top closet, where `t` supplied the variation and masked it.

STATE.md's convention is that incidental fixes ride along with the branch in flight, so I'm fixing it here in its own commit.

feat(settings): the settings screen

Account row, two working preference toggles, the language control, a
read-only location row and sign out. Sign out moves here from the profile
hub, which was holding it only until this route existed.

Two deliberate divergences from Fitcheck.dc.html:782-821. The Pro banner
(:794) is dropped: the profile hub already owns the single Pro entry point
and opens the shared UpgradeSheet, and two cards on two screens can drift
into disagreeing about what Pro is. The account row's chevron (:791) is
dropped because it implies an account detail screen that does not exist --
two bottom-nav tabs used to 404 for that exact reason.

The design's four toggles become two, and both change real behaviour in
this same PR. The daily fit reminder is not among them: it needs web-push,
and no service worker, VAPID keys or scheduler exist, so it ships with the
notifications plan rather than as a switch that schedules nothing.

Toggles are optimistic and revert on a failed write with a visible message.
A switch that waits for a round trip reads as broken; one that stays moved
after a failed save is worse, because the screen then disagrees with the
database and only a refresh reveals it. Track and knob geometry are inline
styles -- arbitrary-value utilities have silently failed to resolve in this
project three times, and a switch whose track collapses is not a switch.
EOF
)" && git log --oneline -4

Read the whole location path. It's the most carefully-guarded code in the app — PR #21 fixed three separate bugs in it — so here's what "properly" actually requires, including one constraint that shapes the design.

**The blocker nobody would guess: timezone.** `saveLocation` persists `location_timezone`, and today that value comes from `fetchForecast` (`&timezone=auto`). So location is only written *after* a successful generate, as a side-effect in `applyResult` (`stylist.tsx:186`). Settings has no generate, so it can't reuse that path.

That matters because `location_timezone` is load-bearing: `localDateFor` and `predictDefaultOccasion` read it, and a null falls back to UTC — which is exactly the bug Decision 5 exists to prevent (a UTC key rolls the daily drop over mid-evening). So Settings cannot write a location without resolving its timezone.

**The fix is a dedicated `setLocation` server action** that fetches the forecast purely to read `timezone`, then persists. One Open-Meteo call, no key, no AI, and it's already cached 30 minutes per rounded coordinate. This is genuinely better than today's design: persistence stops being a side-effect of generating and becomes explicit.

**The shape:**

| Piece | Job |
|---|---|
| `lib/weather/use-location-picker.ts` | The hook: city search, permission probe, `getCurrentPosition`, `locating` / `geoError` / `geoSupported`, and the three refs that guard the silent refresh |
| `components/weather/location-picker.tsx` | The shared menu UI, lifted out of `weather-strip.tsx` |
| `setLocation` (server action) | Resolve timezone → persist → `revalidatePath` both screens |

Sync then falls out of the database rather than being wired: Stylist reads stored location through `resolveLocation` on mount, and `location_source: 'city'` already suppresses the GPS refresh via `geoAllowedRef` — so a city chosen in Settings survives, with no new rule.

**Two things I want your call on before I write a line:**

1. **Own PR, or ride along with Settings?** I'd strongly do it as its own plan and PR. It refactors the exact code PR #21 hardened, and burying that under "feat: settings" makes the diff hard to review and the revert-unit wrong. Settings is finished and green *now*; this would hold it hostage for a day.

2. **Does the weather-pill picker stay?** If Settings gets a real picker, the Stylist pill can either remain as a contextual shortcut (two entry points, one shared component — normal, and the pill is where you *notice* the weather is wrong) or be removed so Settings is the only home. I'd keep both, since they'd share one implementation and can't drift.

My recommendation: **merge Settings with the location row read-only plus a "Change on Stylist" hint, then do location as the next plan straight after.** You get Settings today and the location work done properly tomorrow, instead of one large PR where the risky part is hidden inside the safe part.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

**Stop uploading for two minutes — this is time-critical, and right now it's free to fix.**

## Root cause

`lib/ai/tagging-schema.ts:79`:
```ts
colors: z.array(z.string()).min(1).max(3),   // ← free text
material: z.enum(MATERIALS),                  // ← constrained
texture: z.enum(TEXTURES),                    // ← constrained
```

PR #19 converted `material` and `texture` to enums but **left `colors` as free strings**, while in the same PR adding a 21-colour `ColorPicker`. Its own architecture line claims the opposite: *"vocab.ts becomes the single source for … the colour palette; the two edit surfaces **and the AI schema** all read from it."* The AI schema doesn't. That's the bug — an oversight in #19, not a decision.

So Haiku returns whatever it likes ("khaki", "off-white", "light blue"), and the picker only offers 21 names.

## It's worse than one mismatch — there are **four** colour vocabularies

| Where | Count | Disagrees how |
|---|---|---|
| `TagSchema.colors` | ∞ | unconstrained |
| `vocab.ts COLORS` | 21 | what the user can pick |
| `color.ts NEUTRALS` | 13 | has `khaki`, `ecru`, `gray` — **not pickable**; missing `silver`, `gold`, `camel`, `denim` |
| `color.ts COLOR_FAMILIES` | ~45 | **23 names the picker can never produce** (sand, oatmeal, taupe, ivory, greige, cognac, terracotta, cobalt, midnight, sage, forest, moss, graphite, onyx, jet…) |

And `color.ts:20-23` documents *why* families were widened: *"Item colours come from Haiku as free-form common names … so matching a swatch id verbatim found almost nothing."* That was the right fix **before** a curated palette existed. Now it's papering over the unconstrained schema.

**Real consequences:** `colorHex("khaki")` returns `undefined`, so such an item shows no swatch and the user can't reselect it; and `colorHarmonyScore` treats `silver`/`gold`/`camel` as *accents* while treating unpickable `khaki`/`ecru` as neutrals.

## Why the timing matters

**Your database is empty.** Fixing this now costs nothing. If you upload 30 items first, they get free-text colours and need a normalisation pass — exactly like `scripts/backfill-item-tags.ts` had to do for materials (15 of 29 rows).

## What I'd do — but it's your call, and one part is genuinely yours

1. Constrain `TagSchema.colors` to `z.enum` derived from `vocab.ts COLORS` — the same treatment material/texture got.
2. Derive `NEUTRALS` and `COLOR_FAMILIES` from that palette, with a test asserting every name in them is a real palette colour (the guard `HOT_MATERIALS` already has in `vocab.test.ts`).

**The part I won't decide alone:** which of the 21 count as *neutral*. You know menswear and I'd rather not encode folk rules — `camel` is currently an accent, which for a camel coat seems wrong to me, and `denim`, `silver`, `gold` are all arguable. Tell me your list and I'll pin it with tests.

Also worth your judgement: 21 colours may be too coarse to describe a wardrobe honestly. The alternative is keeping free text and dropping the picker to a *suggestion* list — but then the swatch problem stays. I'd constrain.

Say go and I'll fix it before you upload; say later and I'll write the backfill instead.

All green — 532 tests, tsc clean. Now your question, which is the right one to ask.

**The constraint didn't reduce what *you* can pick.** The picker has offered exactly these 21 since PR #19 — that hasn't changed. What shrank is what *Haiku* could invent, which was unlimited. Before, the AI wrote colours you could never select or see a swatch for; now both sides use one list.

**But your instinct is correct — 21 has real gaps.** The worst:

- **There is no red.** A red sweater gets forced into `rust` or `burgundy`. Both are wrong.
- No **orange**, **purple**, **teal**.
- No **khaki** (a light drab tan — genuinely different from `olive`, which is green), no **taupe**, no **sage**, no light **sky** blue.

The old free-text system hid this: Haiku just wrote "red" and it *looked* fine, while `colorHex("red")` returned undefined, no swatch rendered, and `isNeutral`/`inFamily` both missed it. So the palette was always this small — the gap was just invisible.

Now it's cheap to fix: one list, and tests pin the schema, the picker and the generator families together.

**I'd add 8, taking it to 29:**

| Colour | Neutral? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| red | accent | the outright hole |
| orange | accent | `rust` is a muted earth tone, not orange |
| purple | accent | unrepresented |
| teal | accent | unrepresented |
| khaki | **neutral** | drab tan; pairs like a neutral, distinct from olive |
| taupe | **neutral** | the grey-brown nothing currently covers |
| sage | accent | soft green, very common in knitwear |
| sky | accent | light blue; `blue` reads mid-tone |

**Also, the neutral call I made** (I said I wouldn't decide it alone, then you said go, so here it is explicitly): neutrals are **black, charcoal, grey, white, cream, stone, beige, camel, tan, brown, navy, denim**. Everything else is an accent. The reasoning is that `colorHarmonyScore` gives one accent free and charges 0.25 after — so calling a foundation colour an accent spends that allowance and punishes a restrained outfit, while the reverse only fails to punish. That's why **camel** and **denim** are neutral. Say the word if you'd move any.

content.text:
**Done — upload away.** 532 tests, tsc, build and lint all green.

## Palette: 21 → 42

| Group | Colours |
|---|---|
| Achromatic | black, charcoal, grey, silver, white, ivory, cream |
| Earths | stone, sand, beige, taupe, khaki, camel, tan, **caramel**, **chocolate**, brown |
| Blues | navy, indigo, denim, blue, sky, teal |
| Greens | olive, sage, forest, green, mint |
| Reds/pinks | burgundy, maroon, **red**, rust, terracotta, coral, pink |
| Purples | purple, lavender, plum |
| Yellows/oranges | mustard, yellow, gold, orange |

I stopped short of near-duplicates (ivory/ecru/off-white, burgundy/wine, camel/biscuit) on purpose — when two names describe the same colour the model picks between them at random, and every downstream lookup gets less reliable, not more. Say the word if any specific one you actually own is missing and I'll add it.

## What else changed

- **`ColorPicker` is now typed to the palette**, so the editor can't reintroduce a stray value either — that was the other open door.
- **The item edit sheet drops unknown colours** from legacy `text[]` rows instead of offering them back for re-saving.
- **Neutral vs accent is now explicit.** Foundations count as neutral: navy, indigo, denim, olive, khaki, camel, tan, caramel, chocolate, brown, taupe and the achromatics. Everything else is an accent. This matters because `colorHarmonyScore` gives one accent free and charges 0.25 after — so calling a foundation an accent punishes a restrained outfit, while the reverse only fails to punish.
- **Two of my earlier calls changed** in the process, so you know: **olive is now neutral** (I'd had it as an accent, and with khaki neutral that was inconsistent), and `khaki` — which I used as the example of an *invalid* colour an hour ago — is now a real one.

## One thing to eyeball when you add your first item

The picker panel is `flex-wrap`, so 42 swatches roughly doubles its height. It should wrap fine at 390px, but I haven't seen it on device — the DB is empty, so the capture confirm screen is the first place it renders. **Tell me how it looks on your first upload** and I'll adjust the swatch size if it's cramped.

After that I still owe you: the Location row fix, live verification of both toggles, the rain-guard proof (needs one suede or canvas item), and then the location-picker plan.

### ✅ LIVE-VERIFIED end to end (2026-08-06)

**Rain guard was proven against a real forecast**, not a fixture. Manila was live-rainy (`fetchForecast`
reported `condition: "Rain"`, `rainNow: true`, 26°C); one of the three leather sneakers was temporarily
set to `Canvas`, the location temporarily set to Manila, and today's drop deleted between runs:

| `rainGuard` | Shoes the generator chose |
|---|---|
| `true` | Leather · Leather · Leather — the canvas pair never appears |
| `false` | Leather · Leather · **Canvas** |

That exercises the whole chain: `profiles.preferences` → `readPreferences` → `candidateArgs.rainGuard`
→ `weatherRules` → `eligibleByCategory` → `outfit_items`. **Two real Haiku calls were spent.**

**Fahrenheit was verified on the same screen:** `feels 31°C` rendered as `feels 88°F` (31 × 9/5 + 32 =
87.8). The headline moved 26° → 81° only because the forecast ticked to 27°C between loads.

**The write path was already proven by the user's own taps** — `profiles.preferences` held a written
`{"tempUnit":"C","rainGuard":true}` rather than the `{}` default before any of this testing began.

⚠️ **Synthetic clicks into the Simulator fail on this machine** with System Events `-25204`
(accessibility permission), so toggle taps must be done by hand; DB state is the way to drive
verification instead.

**All test data was reverted**: shoe back to `Leather`, location columns back to null, preferences back
to `{"tempUnit":"C","rainGuard":true}`, and `outfits` / `outfit_items` / `generation_events` cleared so
the user's reroll allowance was not consumed. Verified by query afterwards.

### ⚠️ Arbitrary-value Tailwind failed a FOURTH time on this branch

`ml-[6px]`, `text-[9.5px]` and `align-[1px]` on the Language row's "Soon" badge all silently failed to
resolve — the badge sat flush against the label and read as `DeutschSOON`. Same failure as `size-[32px]`,
`text-[12px]/[1.3]` and `bottom-[6px]`. **It was caught only by screenshotting the simulator**; tests and
tsc were green throughout. The rule holds and is now cheap to state: a NEW arbitrary value carrying
geometry goes in an inline `style`.

### ⚠️ The colour vocabulary was unconstrained — fixed on this branch, and the palette tripled

`TagSchema.colors` was `z.array(z.string())`: the ONLY field PR #19 left free while adding a 21-swatch
picker in the same PR. Its own architecture note claimed *"vocab.ts becomes the single source … and the
AI schema reads from it"* — the AI schema did not. So Haiku emitted names like `light blue` that
`colorHex()` could not render and the user could not reselect, and `lib/generator/color.ts` had widened
its lean families with ~23 free-form names (sand, oatmeal, cognac, terracotta, onyx…) to compensate.
**Four colour vocabularies, none agreeing.**

Now one: `COLOR_NAMES` sits beside `MATERIALS`/`TEXTURES`, the schema is `z.enum` over it, `vocab.ts`
attaches hex + a `neutral` flag, and `NEUTRALS`/`COLOR_FAMILIES` are derived with tests pinning that
every name in them is a real palette colour. `ColorPicker` is typed to the palette; the item edit sheet
narrows legacy `text[]` rows at the boundary.

**The palette went 21 → 42** (user decision — *"we need a lot of colors mate"*). 21 was not honest: it had
**no red at all**, so a red garment was forced into `rust` or `burgundy`. Free text hid that, because
"red" simply rendered no swatch and matched no family. Near-duplicates (ivory/ecru/off-white) were
deliberately NOT added — when two names describe one colour the model picks between them at random and
every downstream lookup gets less reliable.

**Neutral vs accent is a product decision, now explicit.** It drives `colorHarmonyScore`, which gives one
accent free and charges 0.25 after — so calling a foundation colour an accent spends that allowance and
punishes a restrained outfit, whereas the reverse only fails to punish. Neutral: the achromatics plus
`taupe, khaki, camel, tan, caramel, chocolate, brown, navy, indigo, denim, olive`. ⚠️ **`olive` was
flipped from accent to neutral** partway through, once `khaki` joined as a neutral and the pair became
inconsistent.

**One legacy row was normalised:** an Oxford shirt uploaded 21 minutes before the fix landed carried
`light blue`; set to `sky`. Every colour in the closet is now a palette colour. Uploads after the fix
(`sky`, `ivory`) confirm the constraint is live.

### Location in Settings — DECIDED, and it is its own PR

User chose a **real picker in Settings, kept alongside the Stylist's weather pill**, both driven by one
shared component. **Not built on this branch** — it refactors the code PR #21 hardened.

⚠️ **The constraint that shapes it: `saveLocation` persists `location_timezone`, and that value comes
from `fetchForecast`** (`&timezone=auto`), so today location is only written as a side-effect of a
successful generate (`stylist.tsx:186`). Settings has no generate. `location_timezone` is load-bearing —
`localDateFor` and `predictDefaultOccasion` read it and a null falls back to UTC, the exact bug Decision 5
exists to prevent. **So Settings needs a `setLocation` action that fetches the forecast purely to resolve
the timezone**, then persists. One Open-Meteo call, no key, no AI, already cached 30 min per rounded
coordinate. Planned shape: `lib/weather/use-location-picker.ts` (hook) +
`components/weather/location-picker.tsx` (shared UI) + that action. Sync then falls out of the database:
`resolveLocation` already surfaces stored provenance and `location_source: 'city'` already suppresses the
GPS refresh via `geoAllowedRef`.

Interim on this branch: the row shows the **effective** location via `resolveLocation` (it read
`location_label` directly and said "Not set" while the Stylist showed Berlin) plus a "Change it on the
Stylist screen" hint, so it is no longer a dead end.

### Queue #13 `cutout-backfill` now has nothing to convert

No linked remote Supabase project and no Vercel deployment exist, local storage is at 0 legacy files, and
every new upload is already WebP (`lib/images/encode.ts`). The 10 legacy `cutout.png` files
`MONETISATION.md` cites as "the far bigger lever" are gone with the volume. **Move it out of the
execution order and mark it "run only if `.png` cutouts ever appear"** — `encode.ts:48` can still emit PNG

the end of the project by decision on 2026-07-24**, and queue #16 owns the whole-product type audit.

gh pr create --title "feat: settings" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Builds `/settings`: account row, preferences, language, location, sign out. Sign out moves here from the profile hub, which was holding it only until this route existed.

## Toggles

Two ship, and **both change real behaviour in this same PR**.

- **Rain guard** turns off the suede/canvas exclusion in `weatherRules`. It reaches the wet-material list only — the heat exclusions are about comfort at 30°, `needsOuterwear` is about cold, and a switch labelled "never suede in the rain" has no business touching either.
- **Metric units** ships as a real toggle. The plan said not to ("every surface assumes °C"), but only five display sites exist, so `formatTemp` converts at the render boundary and Celsius stays the storage and reasoning unit everywhere — Open-Meteo is requested in it, `weatherRules` compares against it, and the re-rank prompt states it to the model. `laterAdvice` is the one exception and takes the unit as an argument, because it bakes a temperature into prose server-side; its 5° trigger stays Celsius, since the physics is not a preference.

**Auto-log worn looks is deliberately absent.** Opening a look is not wearing it, and `wear_logs` is the foundation of everything Pro sells. **Daily fit reminder is absent too**: it needs web-push, and no service worker, VAPID keys or scheduler exist — plus iOS only delivers push to home-screen-installed PWAs, so the switch would be on and silently do nothing in a Safari tab. It ships with the notifications plan.

Preferences live in one `jsonb` column with defaults in TypeScript, so adding the next one is not a migration. The read path is lenient per-field (one malformed value cannot discard the others); the write path is strict, so garbage is rejected rather than repaired on every later read. Writes are merge-patches, so two open tabs cannot revert each other. Toggles are optimistic and revert on failure with a visible message.

## Divergences from `Fitcheck.dc.html:782-821`

- **No Pro banner** (`:794`). The profile hub owns the single Pro entry point and opens the shared `UpgradeSheet`; two cards on two screens can drift into disagreeing about what Pro is.
- **No chevron on the account row** (`:791`) — it implies an account detail screen that does not exist. Two bottom-nav tabs used to 404 for that reason.
- **Location row** shows the *effective* location via `resolveLocation` and says where to change it. It read `location_label` directly and said "Not set" while the Stylist showed Berlin. A real picker here is its own PR.

## Also on this branch

**Colours were an unconstrained vocabulary.** `TagSchema.colors` was `z.array(z.string())` — the only field #19 left free while adding a 21-swatch picker in the same PR, though its own architecture note claimed the AI schema read from `vocab.ts`. Haiku emitted names like `light blue` that `colorHex()` could not render and the user could not reselect, and `color.ts` had widened its lean families with ~23 free-form names to compensate: four vocabularies, none agreeing. Now one — `COLOR_NAMES` beside `MATERIALS`/`TEXTURES`, schema as `z.enum`, families and neutrals derived, tests pinning that every name in them is a real palette colour, and `ColorPicker` typed to the palette.

**The palette went 21 → 42.** 21 had no red at all, so a red garment was forced into rust or burgundy; free text hid it because "red" simply rendered no swatch and matched no family. Near-duplicates were deliberately excluded — two names for one colour means the model picks at random.

**`neutral` is now explicit per colour**, because `colorHarmonyScore` gives one accent free and charges 0.25 after: calling a foundation colour an accent spends that allowance and punishes a restrained outfit, while the reverse only fails to punish. So navy, denim, camel, khaki, chocolate and the rest of the menswear foundations count as neutral.

**A pre-existing generator defect, present on `main`.** `candidates.ts` indexed shoes at `(t + d * 2) % shoes.length`. With one top, `t` is always 0, so the index reduced to `2d % shoes.length` and never left 0 whenever that length was even — a two-shoe closet could only ever wear the first pair, and the same combo was emitted twice. `decorrelatedStride` picks a stride coprime with the count, keeping shoes off lockstep with bottoms while still visiting all of them. PR #14 measured shoe coverage on a 20-top closet, where the top index supplied the variation and hid this.

## Verification

Rain guard was proven against a live forecast rather than a fixture — Manila was genuinely raining. Same closet, same weather, same day, only the toggle differing:

| `rainGuard` | Shoes chosen |
|---|---|
| `true` | Leather · Leather · Leather — the canvas pair never appears |

content.text:
Nothing to commit — `docs/` is gitignored by design, so the plan and STATE.md stay local-only as intended.

## PR #28 is open

https://github.com/1curafu/Fitcheck/pull/28 — 7 commits, 33 files, mergeable. I've got a monitor watching CI and will report when `verify` lands.

## The plan is written

`docs/superpowers/plans/todo/2026-08-06-location-in-settings.md`, queued as **9c**. Seven TDD tasks. The two parts worth knowing about before you read it:

**1. It's shaped by a constraint, not by preference.** `saveLocation` persists `location_timezone`, and that value only exists as a by-product of `fetchForecast` during a generate. Settings has no generate, and a null timezone falls back to UTC — the exact failure Decision 5 exists to prevent. So Task 1 builds a `setLocation` action that fetches the forecast purely to resolve the timezone. Notably `saveLocation` must *not* also do that fetch: it runs inside `applyResult` where the timezone is already in hand.

**2. I found a decision the plan has to make, which neither of us had considered: the stale drop.** Changing location changes the weather, but today's looks were already composed for the old city and cached under Decision 5. Without handling it, you'd move Manila → Reykjavik and see outfits built for 26°C rain under a strip reading 12°C overcast.

Task 5 decides it: **changing location deletes today's drop so it rebuilds — and the rebuild is free.** Deleting the stored set is precisely what makes the next call a `drop` rather than a `regenerate`, and `MONETISATION.md` §2 says drops are never metered on any tier. You changed a setting; you didn't ask for a reroll. It also has to delete under the *new* timezone's local date, since moving across zones can change what "today" is.

Two things I deliberately kept out of scope, both noted in the plan: reverse geocoding (Open-Meteo has no endpoint, and a third-party one ships your coordinates off-stack — D8), and removing the Stylist's pill, which you already decided stays.

Also updated the plans README: 9b marked built, and `cutout-backfill` moved out of the execution order to "run only if `.png` cutouts ever appear."

gh api -X PUT repos/:owner/:repo/rulesets/19622742 -f enforcement=disabled

**3. Web UI** — Settings → Rules → *main protection* → set **Enforcement status** to *Disabled*, merge, set back to *Active*.

You're right, and I can name the defect precisely: it's a **card inside a card**. The picker was drawn as a floating dropdown that sits *over* the page on the Stylist — its own border, own background, own padding. Nested inside the Location row's card, you get two borders, two surfaces and an inner box floating with margin on all sides. It doesn't belong to the screen.

The extraction itself was right — one behaviour, one component, no drift. What I wrongly shared was the *presentation*.

Two ways to fix it, and they're genuinely different products:

**A. Inline, restyled.** The picker keeps expanding in place, but in Settings it renders with no surface of its own: full-width rows, hairline dividers, same rhythm as the toggles above it (`px-4 py-[15px]`), search field spanning the row, results as label-left / country-right rows — the item-detail spec-table language the README says to derive from. One component, a `variant` prop, behaviour identical.

**B. A bottom sheet.** Tapping Location opens a sheet, like Refine and Upgrade already do. The search field gets room, the results list gets height, and the keyboard has somewhere to go instead of squeezing a nested box. The project already has this pattern and STATE.md documents its z-index rule (`z-[60]`/`z-[70]` above the `z-50` nav).

**I'd take B.** A searchable list of variable length is exactly what a sheet is for, and on a phone the inline version will always feel cramped once four or five cities come back — the row grows, the page reflows under your thumb, and the field can end up under the keyboard. It also matches how you already reach for a picker elsewhere in the app. The cost is that the Stylist keeps its dropdown, so the two screens share the list and its behaviour but present it differently — which is honest, since one is a quick in-context correction and the other is a deliberate settings change.

Which do you want? If B, I'll also make the Stylist's dropdown a sheet later or leave it — separate call.

**Your test passes: the drop is free on the free tier.**

## Two bugs found by driving the real browser

Both were invisible to the test suite — 569 tests were green the whole time.

1. **City search showed results for an earlier keystroke.** Typing "Oslo" fires searches for "Os", "Osl", "Oslo", and whichever *resolved* last won. The list showed Oss and Os de Balaguer under a field reading Oslo. Fixed and re-verified live — "Oslo" now returns Oslo.

2. **The Stylist path doesn't clear the stale drop.** `setLocation` (Settings) clears it; `saveLocation` (the weather pill) doesn't. That's why your Zurich pick left Berlin's 16°C looks in place. **Not fixed yet** — and I want your call, because the fix isn't obvious.

## Why I stopped rather than fixing it

The naive fix breaks things. On the Stylist the order is: pick city → `generate` runs → `applyResult` calls `saveLocation`. If `saveLocation` cleared the drop, it would delete the looks `generate` had *just* stored, and the next load would regenerate — burning a model call every single time you switch city.

The correct fix is one level up: **`generate` should treat a changed location as invalidating today's stored set**, and rebuild instead of reading it. That's a change to the daily-drop logic itself (`lib/outfits/`, Decision 5 territory), not a two-line patch — which is why I'd rather you weigh in than have me quietly rewrite the generator's caching rule.

Two options:

- **Fix it in `generate` now**, on this branch. Consistent with the Settings behaviour, and it closes the bug properly. Costs one extra AI call whenever you actually change city — which is correct, since the old looks were wrong.
- **Its own small plan**, and this PR ships with the Settings path fixed and the Stylist path documented as a known gap.

I lean toward **fixing it now** — shipping a location feature where one of the two entry points leaves stale looks is the kind of gap that gets forgotten. But it touches the generator, so it's your call.

Also worth noting: I saw a **"1 Issue"** badge from the Next dev overlay on `/settings` in Chrome. I haven't looked into it yet — I'll check it either way.

content.text:
**Fixed and proven live on both doors.**

| Path | Result |
|---|---|
| **Settings** → Zurich → Oslo | drop cleared 3→0, rebuilt, `kind: drop` |
| **Stylist pill** → Oslo → Lisbon | looks rebuilt (names changed), weather now Lisbon 20° Clear, `kind: drop` |

Three `drop` events, **zero `regenerate`**, tier `free`. So on the free tier a location change costs nothing from your reroll allowance — through either entry point.

## Why the fix went in `generate`, not `saveLocation`

`saveLocation` runs inside `applyResult`, *after* `generate` has already stored the day's looks. Clearing there would delete what the same call just wrote, and every city switch would generate twice. So `generate` now skips the stored set when the requested location has moved and falls through — and the fall-through path already records a `drop` rather than a `regenerate`, so the rebuild is free by construction rather than by a special case.

## One judgement call I made, which you should sanity-check

**The threshold is 25km, and it's about weather rather than precision.** The Stylist's silent GPS refresh runs on every load, so a tighter bound would make anyone who commutes pay for a fresh generation every morning — while the forecast 10km away is the same forecast, so those looks were never actually wrong. Both doors now use one predicate (`locationMoved`), so they can't disagree about what counts as a move. `locationChanged` is deleted; it was superseded.

If you'd rather any deliberate city pick invalidate regardless of distance, that's a one-line change — but it would also mean GPS drift across a city boundary costs a generation.

**572 tests · tsc clean · build clean.**

Still outstanding from earlier: the **"1 Issue"** badge in the Next dev overlay that I spotted on `/settings` — I haven't looked at it yet, and I'd like to before this branch goes up for review.
what would be better

**Option B is better — invalidate on any deliberate pick, keep the distance rule only for GPS.**

The reason: distance is a *proxy* for intent, and it's the wrong proxy. What actually matters is whether the user asked.

- **A deliberate pick is a statement**: "give me looks for here." If they tap a city 10km away and nothing changes, the app looks broken and gives them no way to tell why. That's the worse failure — silent, and it makes the feature feel unreliable.
- **The GPS refresh is not a statement.** It runs on every load, in the background, and the user never asked for it. That's where the cost risk actually lives, and that's where a threshold belongs.

The 25km rule I shipped applies the same bar to both, which protects against the commute case but buys that protection by ignoring an explicit request.

Cost of switching: near zero. Deliberately picking a city under 25km away is rare, and when it happens the user wanted it.

Concretely, three cases:

| Situation | Signal | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Same place re-picked | rounded coords equal | do nothing — don't throw away today's looks for a no-op tap |
| Different place, deliberate | `source: "city"` | invalidate, rebuild as a free `drop` |
| Different place, GPS | `source: "geo"` | invalidate only past 25km |

The second row covers both the Settings sheet and the Stylist pill. The third covers the silent refresh *and* an explicit "Use my location" tap — which is fine, because if you tap it while standing still, nothing should change anyway.

One honest note: this brings back the "is it literally the same place" check I deleted an hour ago, for the first row. That's a small reversal, but it's load-bearing here — without it, tapping your own city costs you a regeneration.

Adds a real location picker to `/settings`, driven by the same hook and option list the Stylist's weather pill uses, so the two entry points cannot drift.

## The constraint that shaped it

`saveLocation` persists `location_timezone`, and that value only exists as a by-product of `fetchForecast` during a generate — so today location is written as a side-effect of `applyResult`. Settings has no generate, and a null timezone falls back to UTC, which is exactly the failure Decision 5 exists to prevent (a UTC key rolls the daily drop over mid-evening).

So `setLocation` resolves the timezone first, then persists. One Open-Meteo call, no API key, no AI, already cached 30 minutes per rounded coordinate. `saveLocation` deliberately does NOT gain that fetch — it already holds the timezone from the generate that just ran.

Both paths now write through `locationColumns`, so the column set cannot drift between them.

## A sheet, not an inline picker

The first attempt expanded the Stylist's picker inside the Location row and it read as a card inside a card — two borders, two backgrounds, an inner box floating in its own margin. That presentation was drawn for a control that floats *over* the page.

A sheet also fits what this is: a searchable list of unknown length. Inline, the row grows as results arrive and reflows the page under the user's thumb, and the field can end up beneath the keyboard. `RefineSheet` and `UpgradeSheet` already establish the pattern, and tests pin the failure mode `RefineSheet` shipped with — `fixed` not `absolute`, `z-[70]` above the `z-50` nav, nothing left in the tree when closed.

`LocationPicker` gains a `bare` variant that drops its own surface, so what differs between the two screens is presentation only — the behaviour, option markup and a11y semantics are shared. The Stylist keeps its dropdown, which is right: a quick in-context correction and a deliberate settings change are not the same gesture.

## The stale drop — the decision this PR exists to get right

Changing location changes the weather, and today's looks were composed for the old city. Decision 5 caches the drop; caching does not make a 26°C Manila outfit correct under a 12°C Reykjavik sky.

**A location change rebuilds the drop, and the rebuild is free.** `generation_events` records `kind` by whether a stored set already exists, so clearing it is precisely what makes the next call a `drop` rather than a metered `regenerate` — MONETISATION §2, drops are never metered on any tier. The user changed a setting; they did not ask for a reroll.

Two doors, two mechanisms, one predicate:

- **Settings** (`setLocation`) deletes the rows outright, keyed on the NEW timezone — crossing zones can change what "today" is, and deleting under the old key would destroy a past day's history while leaving the stale row untouched.
- **The Stylist** cannot do that: `saveLocation` runs *after* `generate` has stored the day's looks, so clearing there would delete what the same call just wrote and every city switch would generate twice. Instead `generate` skips the stored set when the requested location has moved, and falls through — a path that already records a `drop`.

**Intent decides, not distance.** Distance was only ever a proxy for intent, and the wrong one: someone who taps a city 10km away has asked for looks there, and a screen that does not change reads as broken. `invalidatesDrop` splits three cases — same place never rebuilds (a no-op re-tap is free), a deliberate pick always does however near, and a GPS fix only past 25km. That threshold belongs on GPS alone because the silent refresh runs on every load and nobody asked for it; a commuter must not pay for a generation each morning.

## Two bugs a real browser found that 569 green tests did not

- **City search showed results for an earlier keystroke.** Typing "Oslo" fires searches for "Os", "Osl", "Oslo", and whichever *resolved* last won — the list showed Oss and Os de Balaguer under a field reading Oslo. Responses are now accepted only while their query is still the latest, and clearing the field clears the results.
- **The Stylist path left stale looks in place**, described above.

## Verified live, in Chrome, on the free tier

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Settings: Zurich → Oslo | drop cleared 3→0, rebuilt, `kind: drop` |
| Stylist pill: Oslo → Lisbon | looks rebuilt, screen reads Lisbon 20° Clear, `kind: drop` |
| Stylist pill: Lisbon → Almada (~5km) | looks rebuilt — the case the distance rule alone would have ignored |
| `generation_events` where `kind='regenerate'` | **0** |

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Make "Style an outfit with this" as good as the daily drop. It currently returns one safe
look and then freezes for the rest of the day.

**Architecture:** No new machinery. Task 1 reuses `diversify`, which the daily path already calls and
the styled path does not. Tasks 2–4 widen the styled look from one to a small set and add an explicit

## Why this exists

Written 2026-07-31, after PR #22 shipped the feature and the user asked whether the styled look is

rebuilds from the whole closet with the piece pinned, it does not filter today's looks — but three
things hold it below the daily drop. All three were confirmed against the merged code, not assumed.

This plan was written *after* checking the rest of the queue, specifically so it does not re-decide

content.text:
I need to stop and report a finding rather than ship this.

## Task 1 fixes a problem that doesn't exist

I measured it four ways before believing it. **`diversify` cannot improve a pinned shortlist**, in any closet shape I can construct:

| Closet | pinned combos | Truncated? | Distinct bottoms/shoes BEFORE → AFTER |
|---|---|---|---|
| Your real 21-item | 6 | no | 6/3 → **6/3** |
| 50 pieces (free cap) | 13 | no | 13/13 → **13/13** |
| 38 pieces, 25 bottoms | 25 | **yes** | 20/10 → **20/10** |
| 82 pieces, 40 bottoms | 40 | **yes** | 20/20 → **20/20** |

Identical every time — including the cases where `slice(0, 20)` genuinely truncates.

**Two reasons, both structural:**

1. **`pinned` is almost never longer than 20.** Pinning one garment yields at most `max(#bottoms, #shoes)` combos, because `buildCandidates`' breadth-first walk emits each top once per pass. You'd need 21+ bottoms *or* 21+ shoes before the slice removed anything at all.

2. **Even when it does truncate, there's nothing to reorder.** That same walk already pairs each pass with a different bottom and shoe — the pinned list arrives maximally varied. And `diversify` tiers on *top + bottom* freshness; when you pin a top, every combo shares it, so the tiering collapses to "sort by bottom", which the walk already did.

So the plan's premise — *"the model is choosing between 20 variations of one idea"* — is true of the **daily** path, where the list spans many tops and ranking clusters across them. Pinning collapses exactly that. The README's "cheap real quality win" is wrong, and my own passing tests only prove it on a hand-built ranked list that `buildCandidates` cannot actually produce.

**I haven't committed anything.**

## What I'd do instead

Drop Task 1 and record why in the plan, then go to **Task 3** — *"cached all day with no way to ask for another"*. That's where the "not as good as it can be" feeling you originally reported actually comes from: you tap a second time and the identical look returns with no explanation, while the stylist screen has a visible Regenerate for precisely that situation. Task 2 (one look → two) is the other half.

Both need the ledger, and **queue #8's `kind` column already exists** — it shipped in PR #25 with `'drop' | 'regenerate' | 'styled'`. So the dependency the plan was waiting on is satisfied; Tasks 2–4 are unblocked now.

Your call: drop Task 1, or keep it anyway as consistency insurance in case `buildCandidates` ever changes shape?
if we have it in plan, then we need it, but would it nothing destroy for us now and in the future?
Fair — and it's a good question. Let me answer it with evidence rather than reassurance, because there *is* one real effect I hadn't measured: **order**.

**Can it destroy anything? No, and that's structural.** `diversify` returns `[...tier1, ...tier2, ...tier3].slice(0, n)` — a *permutation* of its input, capped at the same 20. It can't discard candidates, can't shrink the shortlist below what `slice(0,20)` gave, and can't drop the pinned piece, since it only reorders a list `pinItem` already filtered.

When Task 2 raises it to two looks, you specifically want the top of the list maximally distinct so the two options differ — which is exactly what `diversify` does. So Task 1 isn't dead weight; it's a prerequisite that's **invisible until Task 2 lands**. Your instinct to keep it was right.

input.content:
-- A styling returns a SET of looks, not one.
--
-- `outfits_styled_unique (user_id, styled_item_id, generated_on)` allowed exactly
-- one row per piece per local day, which is what bounded a styling to a single
-- look. Widening it needs an ordinal.
--
-- ⚠️ That ordinal is NOT `look_index`, and this is the trap worth reading.
-- Styled rows keep `look_index` NULL on purpose: `outfits_daily_unique` covers
-- (user_id, occasion, generated_on, look_index), and Postgres treats NULLs as
-- distinct, which is the only reason a styled look and the day's drop can share
-- an occasion without colliding. Giving styled rows a real `look_index` would
-- reintroduce that collision — a styled look at index 0 for `work` today would
-- clash with the drop's look 0. So the order lives in its own column.
alter table public.outfits
  add column if not exists styled_index smallint;

-- Existing styled rows are the first look of their set.
update public.outfits
